reconcile.connective: Commentators uniformly split the one English word "tempt" into two senses—solicitation to evil, which God never does, and trial or proving, which is what He did to Abraham.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells lists Genesis 22:1 against James 1:13 as a flat contradiction, pressing that the KJV renders the same root "tempt" in both places and that the two-senses distinction is read into the text to rescue it.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013); skepticsannotatedbible.com

excerpts.excerpt_text: God is said in Gen 22:1 to have "tempted Abraham"; but there the tempting meant is that of trying or proving, not that of seducement.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Names both verses explicitly and resolves the tension with the trying-vs-seducement distinction—the sharpest single statement of the harmonization.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Though the word tempt, from tento, signifies no more than to prove or try, yet as it is now generally used to imply a solicitation to evil, in which way God never tempts any man, it would be well to avoid it here.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: The philological version of the harmonization: the same word covers 'prove/try' and 'solicit to evil,' and only the latter is denied of God in James.

excerpts.excerpt_text: neither tempteth he any man; that is, to sin; he tempted Abraham, to try his faith, love, and obedience to him … but he never tempts or solicits them to sin; temptations to sin come from another quarter
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Ties both passages together in one note—God 'tempts no man' to sin yet 'tempted Abraham' to try him—exactly the distinction the row turns on. Ellipsis joins two on-tension clauses without altering sense.

pd_work.note: JFB's note on James 1:13 directly harmonizes the passage with Genesis 22:1, distinguishing 'trying or proving' from 'seducement.'
